how: A 2026 review pooled 15 trials, published 2007 to 2023, that taught or prompted bundles of habits like keeping track of drinks, pacing or eating. 13 were at US universities, nearly all with students aged 18 to 24. Most programs were short and digital, often mixed with other parts.

Compared with surveys alone, education or other programs, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They said they drank a tiny bit less often. They may have had a tiny bit fewer alcohol problems, but that could be chance.

A 2013 review of 62 studies says that students who reported more habits nearly always also reported drinking less or fewer problems. But most asked about both at one sitting. In one experiment, students told to use more habits said they did, yet didn't drink less.

The 2013 review also describes two day-by-day studies. Students reported drinking less on days they used habits about how they drank, like pacing, but more on days they used habits for limiting or stopping. On days with a designated driver or a friend to go home with, they drank more and had more problems. The review's author thinks people plan those for heavy nights.

how: A 2025 review gathered 35 sources on benzo harm reduction. None compared people who used a habit with people who didn't, or measured harm as a result of one.

On a Swedish forum about flubromazolam, a newer benzo, people wrote of staying home and keeping the drug out of reach while high. They also wrote of using less often and not drinking at the same time. In Canada, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs set up friend groups to check on each other.

In a Baltimore pilot, 103 women who do sex work and use drugs got fentanyl test strips. A month later, 69 in 100 of the 68 followed up said they did something safer after a result, like asking someone to check on them. The number who said they used alone fell from 96 in 100 to 68 in 100, with no comparison group.

In 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl strip went with reports of using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone, a medicine for opioid overdose, nearby over 28 days. The link was strongest when benzos were tested. That's what people said they did, not harm.
